items.readable_text:
Content:
Percentages are very common in everyday life. For example, they are used in retail, finance, and sports! In this lesson, we will learn how to calculate the percentage of a whole number in real-world situations.

Content:
For example, suppose Daniel and Luisa traveled [MATH: 200] kilometers in their car. If Luisa drove [MATH: 40 \%] of the way, how many kilometers did she drive?

Content:
To solve this problem, we can use the following formula:
[MATH: \textrm{part} = \textrm{percentage} \times \textrm{whole}]

Content:
In this case, the whole is the number of kilometers traveled, which is [MATH: 200] kilometers. The percentage is [MATH: 40 \%,] and the part is the distance Luisa drove.

Content:
As usual, we can use two methods to solve this problem:

Content:
Method 1

Content:
First, we convert the percentage to a decimal:
[MATH: 40 \% = 40 \div 100 = 0.4]

Content:
Applying our formula, we have
[MATH: part|= percentage × whole; = 40% × 200; = 0.4 × 200; = 80.]

Content:
So Luisa drove [MATH: 80] kilometers.

Content:
Method 2

Content:
First, we convert the percentage to a fraction:
[MATH: 40 \% = \dfrac{40}{100} = \dfrac{40 \div 20}{100 \div 20} = \dfrac{2}{5}]

Content:
Applying the formula, we get
[MATH: part|= percentage × whole; = 40% × 200; = (2)/(5) × 200; = (400)/(5); = 80.]

Content:
Again, we find that Luisa drove [MATH: 80] kilometers.

sections.normalized_html: In a garden, there are [MATH: 40] flowers, [MATH: 30 \%] of which are roses. How many roses are there in the garden?
sections.readable_text: In a garden, there are [MATH: 40] flowers, [MATH: 30 \%] of which are roses. How many roses are there in the garden?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we can use the following formula: [MATH: \textrm{part}= \textrm{percentage}\times \textrm{whole}]

In our case, the whole is the number of flowers in the garden, which is [MATH: 40] flowers. The percentage is [MATH: 30 \%,] and the part is the number of roses in the garden.

Method 1

First, we convert the percentage to a decimal: [MATH: 30 \% = 30 \div 100 = 0.3]

Applying our formula, we get [MATH: part|= percentage × whole; = 30% × 40; = 0.3 × 40; = 12.]

So, there are [MATH: 12] roses in the garden.

Method 2

First, we convert the percentage to a fraction: [MATH: 30 \% = \dfrac{30}{100} = \dfrac{30 \div 10}{100 \div 10} = \dfrac{3}{10}]

Applying our formula, we get [MATH: part|= percentage × whole; = 30% × 40; = (3)/(10) × 40; = 3 × (40)/(10); = 3 × 4; = 12.]

So, there are [MATH: 12] roses in the garden.
